original_question: Fix r >= 2. How large can lambda_1(G) + lambda_n(G) be among all K_{r+1}-free graphs G of order n?
target_in_paper: Problem 9 (Brandt [27]) in Section 18, "Maximal λ_1 + λ_n of K_{r+1}-free graphs": Let r ≥ 2. How large can λ_1(G) + λ_n(G) be if G is a K_{r+1}-free graph of order n?
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's target almost verbatim: it fixes r ≥ 2, asks for the extremal size of λ_1(G) + λ_n(G), restricts to K_{r+1}-free graphs, and uses order n as the vertex-count parameter. It is neither broader nor narrower than the official Problem 9.
missing_details: The paper's λ_i(G) are the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix A(G), ordered as λ_1(G) ≥ λ_2(G) ≥ ... ≥ λ_n(G).
The paper works throughout with graphs that are simple, undirected, and unweighted.
The phrase "graph of order n" means |V(G)| = n.
The condition "K_{r+1}-free" means that G contains no complete subgraph on r + 1 vertices.
It is implicit that r is an integer with r ≥ 2.

No ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree, nilpotency, or "for all sufficiently large" qualifier is part of this problem; the only hidden assumptions are the graph conventions and the eigenvalue notation.
refined_question: Let r ≥ 2 and n ≥ 1 be integers. For a simple undirected unweighted graph G on n vertices, let λ_1(G) ≥ λ_2(G) ≥ ... ≥ λ_n(G) denote the eigenvalues of its adjacency matrix A(G). What is the maximum possible value of λ_1(G) + λ_n(G) over all K_{r+1}-free graphs G of order n?
justification: The draft clearly targets Section 18 rather than Section 1: it asks exactly about maximizing the sum of the largest and smallest adjacency eigenvalues under a K_{r+1}-free constraint. In the paper this appears as Problem 9, after contextual discussion connecting λ_1(G) + λ_n(G) to Brandt's earlier regular triangle-free problem and noting a related, but not equivalent in full generality, signless-Laplacian variant. The refinement therefore keeps the problem unchanged in scope and only makes the paper's hidden notation and graph conventions explicit.
